hello.note: Polite, for anyone during the day; say it when you walk into a shop. Friends say Ahoj (A-hoy)

how-are-you.note: Polite and the same for anyone

im-well.note: ř is a famous Czech sound: a rolled r and zh said at once

good-morning.note: Early in the morning. Later, Dobrý den

good-night.note: Only when parting at night. Good evening is Dobrý večer (DOB-ree VEH-cher)

please.note: Also means you're welcome, pardon? and here you are

youre-welcome.note: Literally "it's for nothing". Prosím works too

yes.note: Czechs often say just No (no) for yes, which surprises English speakers

excuse-me.note: Sorry, and excuse me to get attention or get past

my-name.note: The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: Polite and the same for anyone

dont-understand.note: The same for a man or a woman

speak-english.note: Polite and the same for anyone. In Prague, many people do

thousand.note: Prices are in crowns, koruny (KO-roo-nih), written Kč

would-like.note: Literally "I'll have...", the usual way to order, the same for a man or a woman. The audio uses kávu (KAA-voo), a coffee

i-want.note: More direct. The audio uses tohle (TO-hleh), this one

discount.note: Prices are fixed in shops; markets are a little more flexible

card.note: Cards work almost everywhere. Change money only at official exchanges, never on the street

toilet.note: Kde (gdeh) means where. Signs say WC, Muži (men), and Ženy (women)

taxi.note: Use an app such as Bolt or Uber, or a taxi company, rather than hailing one in central Prague

train-station.note: Prague's main station is Hlavní nádraží (HLAV-nyee)

which-train.note: After do (do), to, the place changes its ending: Brno becomes Brna (BR-na). The audio uses Brno

buy-ticket.note: In Prague, stamp your public-transport ticket when you first use it

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Brno as the example

trip-length.note: The audio uses Brno as the example
trip-length.spoken: Jak dlouho to trvá do Brna?

allergic.note: Literally "I have an allergy to", the same for a man or a woman. Add the food: ořechy (O-rzheh-khih) nuts, arašídy (A-ra-shee-dih) peanuts, vejce (VAY-tseh) eggs. The audio uses nuts

vegetarian.note: Of dishes. Bez masa (bez MA-sa), without meat

love-dish.note: Literally "it tastes very good to me"

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

beer.note: Czechs drink more beer per person than anyone. A beer mat on the table tells the waiter you'd like another

water.note: Tap water, kohoutková (KO-hoht-ko-vaa), isn't always offered; ask for it

hot.note: Hot, of food and drinks. Hot weather is horko (HOR-ko)

cheers.note: Look each person in the eye as your glasses touch

bill.note: Literally "I'll pay, please", the usual way to ask. Round up or tip about 10%

help.note: Shout it. For any emergency, call 112

need-doctor.note: The same for a man or a woman. For an ambulance, call 155 or 112
